scatterplots-s1.title: Sleep and reaction time
scatterplots-s1.text: A sports science class measures 14 student volunteers: hours of sleep the night before and reaction time, in milliseconds, on a screen test the next morning. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of hours of sleep, 4.5 to 9.5, against reaction time in milliseconds, 281 to 341; the points fall from upper left to lower right in a straight band

scatterplots-s2.title: Outdoor temperature and gas use
scatterplots-s2.text: A homeowner records the average outdoor temperature (degrees Fahrenheit) and the natural gas used for heating (therms) on 16 winter days. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of 16 days: average temperature from 12 to 48 degrees against gas use from 2.1 to 9.8 therms, falling in a straight band, with one point at 20 degrees and 2.1 therms far below the others

scatterplots-s3.title: Age and price of used cars
scatterplots-s3.text: A dealer lists the age (years) and asking price (thousands of dollars) of 16 used cars of one model. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of 16 used cars: age from 1 to 11 years against price from 12.2 to 31.5 thousand dollars; price falls quickly at first and then levels off, a curved pattern

items.q: Which variable is the explanatory variable, and where does it go?

why.correct: Explanatory on the horizontal axis, response on the vertical axis.
options: Right: sleep is thought to help explain reaction time, so it is the explanatory variable, plotted on the x axis.
Reaction time is the response: the class wants to see how it changes with sleep.
Switching the axes changes the picture and the story. The convention puts the explanatory variable on the x axis.
The explanatory variable goes on the horizontal axis; the response goes on the vertical axis.
Hours of sleep, on the horizontal axis
Reaction time, on the horizontal axis
Either one, because the plot is the same both ways
Hours of sleep, on the vertical axis

items.q: What is the direction of the association?

why.correct: Direction: does $y$ tend to rise or fall as $x$ increases?
options: Right: the points fall from upper left to lower right, so larger x values go with smaller y values.
Points need not be on a line to show a clear trend. These clearly fall from left to right.
The points with more sleep sit lower, at shorter reaction times.
"Positive" means both go up together. Here one goes up as the other goes down, which is negative.
Negative: students who slept more tended to have shorter reaction times
There is no direction, since the points do not lie exactly on a line
Negative: students who slept more tended to have longer reaction times
Positive: students who slept more tended to have shorter reaction times

items.q: Which description of the form and strength fits the plot?

why.correct: Form: straight or curved. Strength: how tightly the points follow the form.
options: Right: the points follow a straight band with little scatter around it.
The points do not bend; they follow one straight trend.
Strength is how closely points follow the pattern, not how steep it is.
The scatter around the trend is small compared with the overall drop.
Linear and strong: points stay close to a straight line
Curved and strong: the points bend more and more as sleep increases
Strong, because the trend drops steeply as sleep increases
Linear and weak: the points are scattered far from any pattern

why.correct: Strength, direction, form and unusual features, in context.

strength.label: Strength
options: There is a strong,
There is a weak,
There is a perfect,

why.1: The points stay close to the trend, so the association is strong.
why.2: The points do not lie exactly on a line.

options: negative,
positive,
curved,

why.1: Reaction time falls as sleep rises: negative.
why.2: "Curved" is a form, and the form here is linear.

form.label: Form and context
options: linear association between hours of sleep and reaction time, with no clear outliers.
linear association between the x values and the y values.
linear association, so less sleep causes slower reactions.

why.2: An association from an observational study does not show cause.

conclude.model: There is a strong, negative, linear association between hours of sleep the night before and reaction time for these students, with no clear outliers: students who slept more tended to react faster.

items.q: Which point is unusual, and why?

why.correct: In a scatterplot, an outlier falls far from the overall pattern.
options: Right: it sits well below the pattern; other days near 20°F used about 8 therms.
An outlier in a scatterplot is a point far from the pattern, even if its values are not extreme on either axis alone.
It is at the end of the range, but it sits right on the trend.
It is the largest value, but it fits the pattern: the coldest day used the most gas.
20°F with 2.1 therms: far below other days that cold
There are no unusual points, since each point is between 2 and 10 therms
The day at 48°F with 2.4 therms: the warmest day
The day at 12°F with 9.8 therms: the most gas of any day

items.q: Leaving out the unusual day, how would you describe the association?

why.correct: Describe the pattern of the bulk of the data and mention the outlier separately.
options: Right: the other 15 points fall steadily as temperature rises, close to a straight line.
One unusual point does not erase a clear pattern in the other 15.
As temperature rises, gas use falls, a negative association.
The points follow a straight trend closely, so the association is strong and linear.
A strong, negative, linear association: colder days used more gas
No association, because one day breaks the pattern
A strong, positive, linear association: warmer days used more gas
A weak, negative, curved association

items.q: What is the most likely explanation for the unusual day?

why.correct: Look for a reason behind an outlier; report it.
options: The clear pattern in the other points shows that it does.
The other 15 days show the opposite: colder days use more gas.
It might be an error, but a point should be checked and its removal explained, not dropped silently.
Right: an outlier often has a story; it should be checked and reported, not silently deleted.
Gas use does not depend on the temperature
Colder days use less gas than warmer days do
The temperature was recorded wrong, so the point should be removed without comment
Something else changed, such as the family being away

items.q: Which statement about cause is justified by this plot?

why.correct: Association is not causation, even when a cause is plausible.
options: The direction is backward, and the plot does not show cause at all.
One outlier does not hide a clear association.
An observational plot cannot prove a cause, and the amount saved per degree is a question for a model.
Right: a scatterplot of observational data shows association. Here a cause is believable for other reasons, but the plot by itself does not prove it.
It shows that gas use causes the temperature to change
It shows nothing, since the plot has an outlier
It proves that each degree of warming saves the same amount of gas
Association only; a cause is plausible, but not proven by the plot

items.q: What is the form of the association?

why.correct: Form describes the shape of the pattern: straight or curved.
options: Price falls the whole way; it only falls more slowly for older cars.
Right: the drop from year 1 to year 4 is about 11 thousand dollars, but from year 8 to year 11 it is about 1.5 thousand.
Direction and form are separate features. This negative association has a curved form.
The yearly drop shrinks with age, so the points bend.
Curved: price rises and then falls
Curved: a fast early drop, then a leveling off
No form, because the association is negative
Linear: price drops by the same amount each year

items.q: About how much did price fall from 1-year-old to 4-year-old cars, compared with 8-year-old to 11-year-old cars?

why.correct: Read approximate values off the plot to compare changes.
options: Read the plot: the early drop is several times the late one.
That reverses the two spans: the steep drop is at the young end.
Right: about 30.9 to 20 for the first three years, about 13.7 to 12.2 for the last three.
Those are prices, not drops in price.
About the same, about 6 thousand dollars in each span
About 1.5 thousand dollars, compared with about 11 thousand
About 11 thousand dollars, compared with about 1.5 thousand
About 20 thousand dollars, compared with about 12 thousand

items.q: Which describes the direction and strength?

why.correct: A curved association can be strong.
options: Right: price falls with age, and the points stay close to the bend.
A curved pattern can be strong. Strength is how closely the points follow the pattern, whatever its shape.
Direction is about how $y$ changes as $x$ increases, not the size of the values.
Newer cars costing more is a negative association: as age rises, price falls.
Negative and strong: points follow the curve closely
Negative and weak, because the pattern is not a straight line
Positive and strong, since each price is above 10 thousand dollars
Positive and weak, since newer cars cost more

items.q: A buyer says, "Since the pattern is curved, age and price are not related." What is wrong with this?

why.correct: Form and the existence of a relationship are different questions.
options: Relationships can be curved. This one is strong.
The relationship is negative: older cars cost less.
The pattern really is curved; the problem is the conclusion drawn from it.
Right: price changes with age in a clear, predictable way, only not by the same amount each year.
Nothing; two variables are related just when the pattern is linear
The buyer should have said the relationship is positive
The pattern is linear, so the buyer misread it
A curved pattern is still a relationship, just not a linear one

items.q: A researcher wants to know whether the number of hours a store is open each week helps explain its weekly sales. How should the scatterplot be set up?

options: Each axis shows a different variable.
Right: hours open is the explanatory variable, sales the response.
A scatterplot plots two quantitative variables, one point per store.
That puts the response on the x axis. The variable thought to explain goes on the x axis.
Hours open on both axes
Hours open on the horizontal axis, weekly sales on the vertical axis
One axis for each store, with bars for sales
Weekly sales on the horizontal axis, hours open on the vertical axis

items.q: Which pair of variables could be shown on a scatterplot?

why.correct: A scatterplot needs two quantitative variables on the same individuals.
options: Right: two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals.
Favorite subject is categorical, so a scatterplot cannot show it.
A scatterplot pairs two variables on the same individuals. These are one variable for two groups.
Both are categorical. A two-way table or segmented bar chart fits them.
Height and arm span of 25 students, both in centimeters
Grade level and favorite subject of 25 students
Heights of 25 students in one class and 30 students in another
Favorite sport and eye color of 25 students

items.q: Plot A shows points tightly packed around a gentle upward trend; plot B shows points loosely scattered around a steep upward trend. Which association is stronger?

why.correct: Strength is tightness around the pattern.
options: Positive and negative associations can both be strong.
Right: strength measures how closely points follow the form, not the steepness.
Two positive associations can differ in strength.
Steepness is about how much $y$ changes per unit of $x$, not about strength.
Neither, because strength needs a negative trend
Plot A, because its points are closer to the pattern
Both are equally strong, since both are positive
Plot B, because its trend is steeper

items.q: What does a positive association between two quantitative variables mean?

why.correct: Positive: as $x$ increases, $y$ tends to increase.
options: Association describes a pattern, not cause.
Points can trend upward without lying on a line.
Right: the points trend upward from left to right.
Values can be positive with any direction of association.
Each increase in one causes an increase in the other
The points lie exactly on an upward line
Above-average values of one tend to go with above-average values of the other
Both variables take positive values
